assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new observational window with a detector built from a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice is the kind of instrument-driven discovery I value most: IceCube's 2013 detection of a high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux, then the 2017 TXS 0506+056 association and the 2022 Galactic-plane and NGC 1068 results, founded a new astronomy.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and drove the IceCube concept and led the collaboration's science; Spiering was a founding figure of the neutrino-telescope programme (Baikal, AMANDA, IceCube) and its long-time spokesperson/leader. Both are on the credited list, which gives a two-person prize. Many collaboration members and the AMANDA/DUMAND predecessors also contributed, so the instrument-versus-discovery credit boundary needs care.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels, including by independent analyses. Source identification is still partial (one blazar flare, one Seyfert galaxy, the Galactic plane), but the existence of the new window is firmly established and the field is now maturing, so recognition looks timely.
uncertainties: Individual source associations are at modest significance and could be revised.
Whether a prize should also recognise early pioneers or other collaboration leaders outside the credited list.
I am recalling the milestone dates and the credit history from memory and have not verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol) turned a foundational property of quantum states into a practical route to provably secure communication. It has clear lasting impact, spawned a global experimental field and links directly to the quantum-information theme recognised in recent prizes.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard's 1984 protocol and Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based scheme are the canonical founding works. The list gives Ekert under two spellings; I treat them as one person and use the plain 'Artur Ekert' string. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a historical complication, and he is not on the credited list, so I cannot propose him.
assessment.maturity: Experimental QKD has been demonstrated over fibre and satellite links and entanglement-based tests are well established. Real-world device security and the engineering maturity of deployment are still debated, but the foundational physics is stable. This is outside my own expertise, so I would lean on colleagues in quantum information.
uncertainties: Whether the core contribution is physics or information science and cryptography.
Wiesner's precedence and how a committee would handle it.
Practical security of implementations does not bear on the founding idea but could affect committee appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices became a programmable platform for strongly correlated quantum many-body physics: proposals for realising Hubbard models, the observed superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. It is a mature, widely replicated experimental field with deep links to condensed-matter theory.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) and Cirac supplied key theory for lattice quantum simulation; Bloch is the leading experimentalist for the platform. Greiner and Esslinger also made decisive experimental contributions, so a three-person limit forces a hard choice and I have picked a theory-plus-experiment combination. Cirac and Zoller overlap with another longlist entry on trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum computation theory.
assessment.maturity: The core results are confirmed independently by many groups and the interpretation is stable. Two decades of impact make recognition timely, if not overdue, though the long-term payoff for quantum simulation is still being worked out.
uncertainties: Competing allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac and Zoller, and overlap with the trapped-ion theory entry.
This is outside my own expertise, so I defer partly to colleagues in atomic and condensed-matter physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, giving the most precise measurements humans make and enabling tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. This is a measurement-technique advance that opened new physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock concept and demonstrated the first clock; Ye's group pushed it to the 10^-18 regime with strontium and developed the associated spectroscopy. Both are on the list and this pairing is natural. Competing optical-clock approaches, such as single-ion clocks, and the comb contributions already recognised in 2005 mean credit boundaries must be handled carefully.
assessment.maturity: Several laboratories now report agreement at the 10^-18 level, which is strong independent confirmation, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. The timing looks good.
uncertainties: Overlap with ion-clock work and with the earlier comb prize.
Whether the committee prefers a broader optical-clock citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and precisely measuring antihydrogen and antiprotons gives direct laboratory tests of CPT symmetry and gravity on antimatter. As someone who has measured cosmic-ray antimatter, I value the patient control of systematics here: spectroscopy of the 1S-2S line, hyperfine structure and a gravity measurement are real achievements.
assessment.attribution: Hangst led ALPHA, which trapped and spectroscopically probed antihydrogen; Gabrielse led ATRAP and made the extremely precise antiproton and positron/electron magnetic-moment measurements. The prize could reasonably go to this pair. Other collaborations (ATHENA, ASACUSA, AEgIS, BASE) also contributed, and that is a credit boundary the credited names do not settle.
assessment.maturity: Results are reproducible between groups and improve in precision, but no deviation from CPT has been found, so the discovery is a precision null result rather than a new effect. That may make the committee ask whether a prize is premature or whether the technique is a sufficient basis.
uncertainties: Null results can weaken the case for a prize.
The balance of credit among ALPHA, ATRAP, ATHENA, ASACUSA and BASE groups.
Details of the latest numerical results are quoted from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Imaging the shadow of the M87 and Sgr A* black holes with a planet-sized VLBI array is a technical tour de force and a clear, striking measurement that tests general relativity in the strong-field regime. The calibration, imaging and systematics effort is exactly the sort of patient instrument work I respect.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT collaboration's technical development and Moran contributed the VLBI foundations, but the result came from a collaboration of well over 200 members. Three people cannot fairly capture it, and the allocation of credit is clearly unresolved.
assessment.maturity: M87 imaging has been reproduced in repeated observing campaigns and Sgr A* gives a second independent source, but the physical parameters (spin, jet launching) are still model-dependent. The interpretation is not yet fully settled.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit and the three-person limit.
Model dependence of the inferred spin and the imaging algorithms.
Whether the timing is premature relative to better future images.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at ATLAS and CMS completed the Standard Model and was an enormous detector and data-analysis achievement. I hold instrument building in high regard, and these experiments were its largest-scale expression. The 2013 prize already recognised the theoretical prediction, so the question is whether the experimental side should now be honoured.
assessment.attribution: Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at announcement), Jenni (ATLAS founding spokesperson) and Della Negra, Virdee (CMS) are the typical credited names. The list has four, so one must be left out; I choose Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee as a balanced ATLAS/CMS selection, noting that Della Negra has an equally strong claim for CMS. Thousands of collaborators and the question of whether to honour the LHC construction instead make the allocation truly difficult.
assessment.maturity: The discovery is confirmed beyond doubt by two independent experiments and subsequent properties measurements. Recognition may be considered more complete after 2013, which could weigh against a second prize in this area.
uncertainties: The 2013 prize may be seen as having discharged the committee's duty on the Higgs.
Which four-person set best represents ATLAS and CMS; Della Negra is omitted only for the three-name limit.
Overlap with the entry on LHC and detector construction.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and pixel detectors transformed particle tracking and vertexing, enabling heavy-flavour physics, the top quark and Higgs analyses, and also spreading to X-ray and space instrumentation. As a detector builder I know how decisive this technology is, and it has had lasting impact across experiments.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer's planar process for silicon detectors, Parker's microstrip work and Heijne's pixel developments are plausible decisive contributions. Other pioneers, such as the hybrid-pixel and CCD vertex detector developers, likely also deserve consideration, and the supplied names may not cover all of them.
assessment.maturity: The technology has been used for decades in every collider and is firmly established. The Nobel committee has recognised instrumentation before (Charpak 1992), so this is plausible, but the discovery is an enabling technology rather than a single result.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a prize for an enabling technology rather than a discovery.
Credit among silicon-detector pioneers beyond the three listed.
Historical credit details are from memory.
